units.text: INT. WOMAN - CONTINUOUS

Politics are in a sad way everywhere, I am told. They certainly are in England. Dear Mr. Cardew is ruining the country. I wonder Mrs. Cardew allows him. I am sure, Lord Illingworth, you don’t think that uneducated people should be allowed to have votes?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I think they are the only people who should.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: Do you take no side then in modern politics, Lord Illingworth?
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: One should never take sides in anything, Mr. Kelvil. Taking sides is the beginning of sincerity, and earnestness follows shortly afterwards, and the human being becomes a bore. However, the House of Commons really does very little harm. You can’t make people good by Act of Parliament,—that is something.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: You cannot deny that the House of Commons has always shown great sympathy with the sufferings of the poor.
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: That is its special vice. That is the special vice of the age. One should sympathise with the joy, the beauty, the colour of life. The less said about life’s sores the better, Mr. Kelvil.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: Still our East End is a very important problem.
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: Quite so. It is the problem of slavery. And we are trying to solve it by amusing the slaves.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: Certainly, a great deal may be done by means of cheap entertainments, as you say, Lord Illingworth. Dear Dr. Daubeny, our rector here, provides, with the assistance of his curates, really admirable recreations for the poor during the winter. And much good may be done by means of a magic lantern, or a missionary, or some popular amusement of that kind.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I am not at all in favour of amusements for the poor, Jane. Blankets and coals are sufficient. There is too much love of pleasure amongst the upper classes as it is. Health is what we want in modern life. The tone is not healthy, not healthy at all.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: You are quite right, Lady Caroline.
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: I believe I am usually right.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: Horrid word ‘health.’
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Silliest word in our language, and one knows so well the popular idea of health. The English country gentleman galloping after a fox—the unspeakable in full pursuit of the uneatable.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: May I ask, Lord Illingworth, if you regard the House of Lords as a better institution than the House of Commons?
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: A much better institution, of course. We in the House of Lords are never in touch with public opinion. That makes us a civilised body.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: Are you serious in putting forward such a view?
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: Quite serious, Mr. Kelvil.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: To MRS. ALLONBY.

Vulgar habit that is people have nowadays of asking one, after one has given them an idea, whether one is serious or not. Nothing is serious except passion. The intellect is not a serious thing, and never has been. It is an instrument on which one plays, that is all. The only serious form of intellect I know is the British intellect. And on the British intellect the illiterates play the drum.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: What are you saying, Lord Illingworth, about the drum?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I was merely talking to Mrs. Allonby about the leading articles in the London newspapers.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: But do you believe all that is written in the newspapers?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I do. Nowadays it is only the unreadable that occurs.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: Rises with MRS. ALLONBY.
Are you going, Mrs. Allonby?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Just as far as the conservatory. Lord Illingworth told me this morning that there was an orchid there as beautiful as the seven deadly sins.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: My dear, I hope there is nothing of the kind. I will certainly speak to the gardener.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Exit MRS. ALLONBY and LORD ILLINGWORTH.
Remarkable type, Mrs. Allonby.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: She lets her clever tongue run away with her sometimes.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Is that the only thing, Jane, Mrs. Allonby allows to run away with her?
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: I hope so, Caroline, I am sure.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Enter LORD ALFRED.
Dear Lord Alfred, do join us. [LORD ALFRED sits down beside LADY STUTFIELD.]
You believe good of every one, Jane. It is a great fault.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: Do you really, really think, Lady Caroline, that one should believe evil of every one?
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: I think it is much safer to do so, Lady Stutfield. Until, of course, people are found out to be good. But that requires a great deal of investigation nowadays.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: But there is so much unkind scandal in modern life.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: Lord Illingworth remarked to me last night at dinner that the basis of every scandal is an absolutely immoral certainty.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: Lord Illingworth is, of course, a very brilliant man, but he seems to me to be lacking in that fine faith in the nobility and purity of life which is so important in this century.
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: Yes, quite, quite important, is it not?
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: He gives me the impression of a man who does not appreciate the beauty of our English home-life. I would say that he was tainted with foreign ideas on the subject.
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: There is nothing, nothing like the beauty of home-life, is there?
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: It is the mainstay of our moral system in England, Lady Stutfield. Without it we would become like our neighbours.
units.name: KELVIL
